analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workers' rights to form unions, strike, and sue employers who break labor law.
analysis.headline: The Senate labor-organizing bill, backed by 41 Senate Democrats, never received a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it easier for workers to join together in unions. It would ban companies from permanently replacing strikers, prohibit mandatory anti-union meetings, limit forced arbitration agreements that block class-action lawsuits, expand penalties for employers who fire or retaliate against workers, and let workers sue employers directly in court. It also would override state right-to-work laws and make companies that share control over workers jointly responsible for labor violations. The bill was introduced by Senator Patty Murray with 41 Democratic and allied cosponsors and was sent to the Senate labor committee, where it never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to organize or join unions would gain the most: stronger protection from being fired or permanently replaced for union activity, faster union elections, binding arbitration to force a first contract, and larger penalties on employers who break the law. Workers harmed by forced arbitration clauses would regain the right to join class lawsuits, and workers in right-to-work states could be covered by fair-share fee agreements.

how_it_helps.text: Bars employers from permanently replacing striking workers or discriminating against them when they return, protecting the right to strike.

Makes it an unfair labor practice to force employees to attend anti-union meetings and bans companies from using forced arbitration agreements to block workers from joining class or collective claims.

Expands who counts as an 'employee' under labor law, preventing employers from classifying workers as independent contractors or low-level supervisors outside the law's protections, and broadens the joint-employer standard so companies that share control over workers can be held responsible.

Imposes civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation (up to $100,000 for repeat violations), makes NLRB orders self-enforcing, and lets individual workers sue in federal court for back pay, double damages, and punitive damages when they are fired or suffer serious economic harm.
Speeds up union elections, removes employers' ability to intervene in representation cases, and requires binding arbitration if the two sides cannot agree on a first contract after mediation.
Overrides state right-to-work laws so unions and employers can agree that all workers covered by a contract pay a fair-share fee for the representation they receive.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially large companies and industries with histories of opposing unions — would bear new civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation (up to $100,000 for repeat violations), expanded personal liability for executives, joint-employer liability, and binding arbitration of first contracts. Companies would also lose the ability to permanently replace strikers, hold mandatory anti-union meetings, or use arbitration agreements to prevent class claims.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state right-to-work laws, which currently bar contracts requiring all employees in a union workplace to pay fees; critics argue this compels workers who choose not to join a union to fund it.

If negotiations for a first contract stall, a three-member arbitration panel — one member chosen by the union, one by the employer, one neutral — could impose a binding two-year contract on both sides, removing that decision from the parties themselves.

The bill imposes civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation (doubled to $100,000 for repeat violations) and potential personal liability for company directors and officers, a significant cost and liability expansion for employers large and small.
The revised 'employee' test would reclassify many independent contractors as employees covered by labor law, a change opponents said threatened genuine self-employment and gig-work arrangements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits for workers are large: union members earn significantly more than non-union workers, and the bill targets the specific tactics — firings, permanent replacements, captive-audience meetings, misclassification, arbitration agreements — that make organizing risky today. The main costs and objections fall on employers: the bill overrides state right-to-work laws, restricts employers' ability to replace strikers, mandates binding arbitration of first contracts, and imposes penalties up to $100,000 per violation plus expanded personal liability for officers. Supporters see those as deterring law-breaking; opponents see them as tilting bargaining decisions away from employers and workers who prefer non-union workplaces. The bill never got a Senate debate or vote, so its provisions were never tested against amendments; as written it is a decisive shift of labor-law leverage toward unions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died without a vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 2, 2019, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate HELP Committee the same day.
That referral was the last action the bill ever received; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed in the 116th Congress.
All 41 of its cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents, and no Republican signed on, so the bill had no path to the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster in the Senate.
The bill would have amended the National Labor Relations Act to expand penalties for violations, let workers sue employers directly, and bar the permanent replacement of striking workers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who benefit from the current labor-law balance are better off; the bill died in committee without ever reaching a vote, so no provision limiting striker replacement, mandatory anti-union meetings, or forced arbitration took effect.

for.name: 40 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and every other listed Democratic senator.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 41 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Senate majority never brought the bill to the floor; business groups opposed comparable legislation.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents; no Senate Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding the majority the bill never moved past referral to the HELP committee.

industries.industry: Employers and business associations (retail, manufacturing, gig platforms, franchise chains)
industries.note: The bill strips away the main legal tools companies use to resist unionization: permanent striker replacement, mandatory anti-union meetings, misclassification of workers as contractors, forced arbitration of class claims, and slow election and bargaining tactics. It also imposes civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, personal liability for officers, and joint-employer exposure for companies that rely on contractors and franchises.

The bill strengthens unions' organizing and bargaining position, allows fair-share fee agreements overriding state right-to-work laws, and gives unions access to employee contact lists during elections. Workers who want to organize gain alongside the unions that would represent them.
